The initial body mass of a newborn Bare-tailed woolly opossum (Caluromys philander) is remarkably small, weighing just 0.2 grams [Wwb = 0.2 grams] at the moment of parturition. This altricial neonate, born after a brief gestation period documented at an average body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], requires approximately 24 days [tg = approximately 24 days] of intrauterine development before emerging to begin its protracted dependency on maternal care. The gestation time (24 days) [tg = 24 days] is notably short even among didelphids, a factor that constrains the degree of organ system maturation achieved prior to live birth at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. Following emergence, the offspring enter a vulnerable stage as suckling juveniles, entirely dependent on the mother's milk while their sensory and motor systems continue to develop. The mother's ability to provision these tiny neonates depends critically on her capacity to meet the elevated energetic demands of lactation, a challenge further compounded by the need to periodically forage for her own sustenance within the forest canopy.

The dependent period of the offspring is characterized by a specific developmental timeline. The time since birth at weaning for this species has been recorded as 100 days [tx = 100 days] when measured at a steady core temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This extended period of milk dependency is typical of marsupials, during which the young undergo substantial growth within the maternal pouch. At the point of weaning, the juvenile opossums have achieved a wet weight at weaning of approximately 11 grams [Wwx = approximately 11 grams], representing a substantial increase from the neonatal mass. This transition to nutritional independence marks a critical phase in the life history, as the young must now forage for solid food items including fruits, nectar, and small invertebrates. The post-weaning period is a time of rapid growth and continued development, as the juveniles refine their locomotory and foraging skills before reaching the next major life history milestone.

Sexual maturation in female Bare-tailed woolly opossums occurs after an extended period of juvenile development. The time since birth at puberty for females is 304 days [tp = 304 days] under ambient thermal conditions that maintain a core body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively late onset of reproductive capability, at nearly one year of age, is balanced by a considerable adult lifespan. The maximum recorded longevity for Caluromys philander reaches 8.9 years [am = 8.9 years] when maintained at a physiological temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This exceptional longevity (8.9 years) [am = 8.9 years] exceeds that of many similar-sized didelphids by a factor of two or more at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. Female adult body size is a key determinant of fecundity, and the ultimate wet weight for females has been measured at around 350 grams [Wwi = around 350 grams], although the species displays considerable intraspecific variation, with published accounts on Animal Diversity Web noting a range from 140 to 390 grams for adult body mass.

Reproductive output in this species reflects a strategy of moderate investment per litter coupled with multiple annual breeding opportunities. Field data indicate that females typically produce 4.5 young per litter [N_R_i = 4.5 young per litter], with the capacity to rear up to 2 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 2 litters per year] under favorable environmental conditions. This reproductive schedule, recorded in populations active at a body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], allows for a substantial annual recruitment potential. The energetic demands of producing and provisioning multiple litters are considerable. At a female body size of approximately 300 grams, field measurements of daily food intake have been estimated at 300,000 joules per day . This high daily energy requirement (300,000 joules per day)  underlies the species' frugivorous and nectarivorous dietary habits, which provide the rapidly assimilable carbohydrates needed to sustain both maternal metabolism and milk production.

The reproductive strategy of this species must be contextualized within its broader ecological niche as an arboreal frugivore inhabiting Neotropical forests. The maximum reproductive rate, which can be reconstructed from the combination of litter size and annual frequency, supports a life history that is notably slower and longer-lived than that of many comparably sized terrestrial didelphids like the Virginia opossum. The extended juvenile period and relatively late female puberty (304 days since birth) [tp = 304 days since birth] are characteristic of species that invest in survivorship and adult body size maintenance over rapid population turnover at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. Female opossums that achieve the upper range of adult body mass near 350 grams [Wwi = 350 grams] are likely to enjoy higher fecundity and greater offspring survival, as body size in marsupials correlates positively with pouch capacity and milk output. The species' ability to maintain a stable core temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] is essential for the proper progression of all developmental and physiological processes, from the brief gestation (24 days) [tg = 24 days] through the dependent juvenile period to the achievement of reproductive maturity and the eventual completion of the maximum lifespan (8.9 years) [am = 8.9 years].
